Find cells outside the table in an Excel workbook

Source: R/inspect_excel.R
inspect_excel.Rd

Lists the blocks of non-empty cells that lie outside the area being read: a note under the table, a total row set apart by an empty row, a second table to the right, a title above. Returns an empty tibble when there are none, so it can be used as a checkpoint.

Usage

inspect_excel(path, sheet = NULL, range = NULL, table = NULL, skip = 0)

Arguments

path

Path to an Excel file (.xlsx, .xlsm or .xls).

sheet

Sheet names or positions. NULL (default) means every sheet.

range

The area to read, where the default NULL finds the table on each sheet. One range, such as "B3:F40" (with a single sheet) or "Sheet1!B3:F40"; or one per sheet as a named vector, c(Sheet1 = "B3:F40", Sheet2 = NA), where NA means find the table. Sheets not named are found automatically.

A range can also be a named range from the workbook (Formulas > Name Manager), such as "Sales". A name carries its own sheet, so range = c("Sales", "Costs") reads both, named by the names, wherever they are; in a per-sheet vector the name must lie on that sheet. Named ranges need an .xlsx file and the xml2 package.

table

Names of defined Excel tables (Insert > Table), or TRUE for all of them. Cannot be combined with sheet or range. .xlsx and .xlsm only, and needs the xml2 package.

skip

Rows at the top of each sheet to leave out before the table is found, as in readxl::read_excel(). Not used for a given range or table.

Value

A tibble with one row per block outside the read area: sheet, area (the area read, such as "B3:F40" or "Sales (B3:F40)"), block (the block's range), position ("title", "above", "below", "left", "right", a combination such as "below right", or "around" for a block that wraps a corner), cells (non-empty cells in the block) and first (the first value in the block, for recognition).

Details

Why this exists. readxl reads the smallest rectangle that holds every non-empty cell on a sheet. A source note three rows under the table therefore becomes extra data rows, and a comment two columns to the right becomes a column named ...7, without a warning. With a range, the opposite happens: cells outside it are dropped without a word. Either way the surprise is silent, and it is cheap to rule out by looking at where the cells actually are.

Finding the table. Without a range for a sheet, the table is the largest block of cells that is not split by an entirely empty row or column, which is what a person looking at the sheet would call the table. Single-cell rows on top of it, such as a title with no empty row below it, are left out, so the header is the first row of the area. This is the area read_workbook() reads by default.

Reporting. Cells outside the area are grouped into blocks the same way and reported with their position relative to the nearest area. A block above the table with at most one cell per row, in any column, is reported as a "title". When reading by table, cells that belong to any defined table on the sheet are never reported, so two tables side by side do not report each other.

Only cells with a value count; formatting, borders and empty strings do not. The cells are found with readxl itself, reading the sheet once as text, so the check costs about one extra read and agrees with readxl on what is empty.

See also

read_workbook(), which reads the same areas and runs this check.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
inspect_excel("data/report.xlsx")
inspect_excel("data/report.xlsx", table = TRUE)

inspect_excel("data/report.xlsx", range = "Sheet1!B3:F40") |>
  expectr::expect_empty(warn_msg = "cells outside the table")
} # }
